cartoes.conceito: Length and unpredictability matter more than swapping letters for symbols.
cartoes.enunciado: An attacker tries billions of combinations per second. Which of these holds out the longest?

opcoes.texto: P@ssw0rd!
Liverpool2024
horse-stapler-battery-cloud
Qw3rty!!

cartoes.explicacao: Four random words make a long, unpredictable phrase. Swapping a for @ does not help: those swaps are already in attackers' dictionaries.

cartoes.titulo: From the strongest second factor to the weakest
cartoes.conceito: Not every second factor protects you equally: the ones that resist phishing come out on top.
cartoes.enunciado: Order these ways of signing in to an account, from most secure to least secure.
cartoes.explicacao: Security keys and passkeys do not work on a fake site, so they resist phishing. SMS can be hijacked with a SIM swap, but it is still better than a password alone.

cartoes.conceito: Password spraying: trying one common password on many accounts avoids the lockout after failed attempts.
cartoes.enunciado: An attacker tries 'Summer2026!' just once on each of Atlas Corp's 5,000 accounts. What is this attack called?

opcoes.texto: Brute force on a single account
Password spraying
Keylogger
SIM swap

cartoes.explicacao: Because each account fails only once, the lockout never triggers. Reject common passwords at sign-up and require MFA.

cartoes.conceito: A password manager creates and stores a unique, strong password for every site.
cartoes.enunciado: You have 80 online accounts. What is the safest way to have a different password for each one?

opcoes.texto: A notebook on your office desk
A spreadsheet called passwords.xlsx
A password manager protected by a passphrase and MFA
One base password with the site name at the end

cartoes.explicacao: The manager generates long random passwords and you only have to remember one passphrase. Protect it with MFA, because it becomes the key to everything.

cartoes.conceito: MFA combines factors of different types: something you know, something you have and something you are.
cartoes.enunciado: A password is something you know. A fingerprint is something you are. And a physical key or your phone is something you…?
cartoes.explicacao: Combining different types of factor forces the attacker to steal two different things. Two passwords in a row are still just one type of factor.

cartoes.titulo: The password policy has bad rules
cartoes.conceito: Forced changes and password hints make passwords weaker, not stronger.
cartoes.enunciado: Atlas Corp published this policy. Which rules go against current best practice?
segmentos: Passwords must be changed every 30 days.
Allow pasting the password into the login field.
Reject passwords that appear in known breaches.
Show a password hint on the login screen.
cartoes.explicacao: People forced to change end up with Summer2025!, Summer2026!, and the hint mostly helps the attacker. Change a password only when there are signs of a breach, and allow pasting so password managers work.

cartoes.conceito: Credential stuffing: email and password pairs stolen from one site are tried on many others.
cartoes.enunciado: Order the stages of this attack, from first to last.

itens.texto: They get into the accounts where the password was reused
Attackers try the pairs on shops, banks and email
A forum suffers a breach of emails and passwords
The list of pairs is sold or published

cartoes.explicacao: The attack only works where the password is reused. A different password on every site, plus MFA, stops it.

cartoes.titulo: Your email showed up in a breach
cartoes.conceito: When an account shows up in a breach, change the password on that site and everywhere it was reused.
cartoes.enunciado: A breach-checking service says your email appeared in a breach of an online shop. What do you do first?

opcoes.texto: Delete the email account and create a new one
Change the password for that shop and wherever I reused it
Nothing, the breach was months ago
Reply to the alert with my password to confirm

cartoes.explicacao: Breach lists circulate for years, so the exposed password is no longer safe to use. Change it wherever it is reused and turn on MFA for those accounts.

cartoes.conceito: The true answers to security questions can often be found on social media.
cartoes.enunciado: A site asks for an answer to 'Name of your first pet'. What is the best option?

opcoes.texto: The pet's real name
A made-up random answer, stored in the password manager
The pet's name with 123 at the end
The same answer I use on other sites

cartoes.explicacao: Anyone who follows you on social media may know your pet's name. Treat the answer like a password: random and stored in the manager.

cartoes.conceito: A passkey replaces the password with a key pair: the private key never leaves your device.
cartoes.enunciado: What is the name of the credential that replaces the password with a key pair stored on your phone or computer?
cartoes.explicacao: A passkey only works on the real domain and the server stores only the public key, so there is no secret to steal. Turn it on for the sites that offer it.

cartoes.conceito: Look-alike domains swap a letter or add a hyphen to fool people who read quickly.
cartoes.enunciado: Banco Luz uses the domain bancoluz.example. Which of these links really goes to the bank?

opcoes.texto: https://bancoIuz.example/login
https://banco-luz.example/login
https://bancoluz.example/login
https://bancolux.example/login

cartoes.explicacao: In a there is a capital I instead of the l, in b an extra hyphen and in d an x at the end. Read the domain letter by letter or, better, use a saved bookmark.

cartoes.conceito: Urgency and links to another domain are the most common signs of phishing.
cartoes.enunciado: This email arrived today. What is the strongest sign that it is phishing?

cenario.label: Inbox
lines: Subject: Your package has been held
Pay €1.99 within the next 2 hours or the package will be returned.

opcoes.texto: The amount is small
The 2-hour deadline and the link to another domain
The email has a subject line
It mentions a package

cartoes.explicacao: Urgency is there to stop you thinking, and the link goes to sp-payments.test, which does not belong to SwiftPost. Open the official site yourself and check the package there.

cartoes.conceito: A double extension hides a program behind a name that looks like a document.
cartoes.enunciado: These attachments came from a supplier. Which one is a disguised program?
cartoes.explicacao: What counts is the last extension: .exe is a program. Turn on the option to show file extensions and never open programs received by email.

cartoes.conceito: The sender name is free text; what counts is the domain after the @.
cartoes.enunciado: Banco Luz only sends emails from @bancoluz.example. Which senders are fake?
cartoes.explicacao: Anyone can put 'Banco Luz' as the name. Look at what comes after the @: only bancoluz.example belongs to the bank.

cartoes.titulo: The QR code stuck on the parking meter
cartoes.conceito: Quishing: a fake QR code stuck over the real one leads to a fake payment site.
cartoes.enunciado: There is a sticker with a QR code to pay on the parking meter. The QR code opens parking-pay.test and asks for your card details. What do you do?

opcoes.texto: Pay, it's faster
Pay at the machine or in the official parking app
Scan the QR code with another app
Pay and keep the receipt

cartoes.explicacao: A QR code is just a link you cannot read before opening it. Be suspicious of stickers and pay through the official channels.

cartoes.titulo: Read the URL in the right order
cartoes.conceito: The domain is what sits between :// and the first slash; it tells you who owns the site.
cartoes.enunciado: Order the parts of this URL, from left to right: https://bancoluz.example/login?ref=email
cartoes.explicacao: Only the domain tells you who controls the site; the path and the parameters can contain any text, even 'bancoluz'. Find the domain before you trust a link.

cartoes.conceito: The text of a link can show one address and take you to another.
cartoes.enunciado: In an email, the link shows one address, but when you hover over it the browser shows another. Which domain will you open if you click?
cartoes.explicacao: The link text is just text; the real destination is what the browser shows on hover. On a phone, press and hold the link to see it before opening.

cartoes.conceito: The macros in a document are code; enabling them can install malware.
cartoes.enunciado: A document received by email says: 'Enable content to view the invoice.' What do you do?

opcoes.texto: Enable it, otherwise I can't see the invoice
Close it and check with the sender through another channel
Forward it to a colleague to open
Save it and open it later

cartoes.explicacao: A real invoice does not need macros to be read. Close the file and check with the sender by phone or through the official portal.

cartoes.conceito: Smishing: the same trick as phishing, but by SMS, where the link is harder to see.
cartoes.enunciado: This SMS arrived on your phone. Which parts are signs of smishing?
segmentos: Package SP-4471 could not be delivered.
No reply within 12h and it will be returned.
cartoes.explicacao: The link points to a strange domain and the short deadline is there to make you act without thinking. Open the official app or site and look up the tracking number there.

cartoes.titulo: The app wants access to your email
cartoes.conceito: Consent phishing: instead of your password, the attacker asks you to authorize an app to get into your account.
cartoes.enunciado: When you open a shared PDF, an app asks to: 'Read, send and delete emails on your behalf'. What do you do?

opcoes.texto: Accept, every app asks for this
Refuse and report it: a PDF reader does not need your email
Accept and change my password afterwards
Accept just this once

cartoes.explicacao: The authorization gives the app its own token, which can stay valid even after you change your password. Refuse requests that ask for too much and revoke suspicious apps in your account settings.

cartoes.conceito: Gluing user text into an SQL query lets the attacker rewrite the query.
cartoes.enunciado: This login code goes to production tomorrow. Which line allows SQL injection?
segmentos: const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'";
cartoes.explicacao: By pasting the email into the SQL, the attacker can close the quote and add ' OR '1'='1. Use parameterized queries: db.query('… WHERE email = ?', [email]).

cartoes.conceito: Putting user text into innerHTML lets the browser run code hidden in that text.
cartoes.enunciado: This code shows comments on a page. Which line allows XSS?
cartoes.explicacao: A comment like runs code in the browser of whoever reads it. Use textContent, which shows the text without interpreting it as HTML.

cartoes.conceito: CSRF: another site makes your browser send a request with your session, without you knowing.
cartoes.enunciado: You are logged in to Banco Luz. A malicious site has a hidden form that sends a POST to bancoluz.example/transfer. What stops the attack?

opcoes.texto: The bank's site using HTTPS
An anti-CSRF token in the form and SameSite cookies
A longer password
Hiding the form's URL

cartoes.explicacao: The malicious site does not know the form's secret token, and with SameSite the browser does not send the session cookie with that request. Use both.

cartoes.conceito: IDOR: the server returns an object by its id alone, without checking that it belongs to whoever is asking.
cartoes.enunciado: Any logged-in customer can see another customer's invoice by changing the number in the URL. Which line causes the problem?
segmentos: const invoice = await db.invoices.findOne({ id: req.params.id });
cartoes.explicacao: Being logged in is not enough: the owner check is missing. Look it up with findOne({ id: req.params.id, customerId: req.user.id }) so each customer sees only their own invoices.

cartoes.titulo: Where do you go after logging in?
cartoes.conceito: Open redirect: the site redirects to any address that comes in the URL.
cartoes.enunciado: After login, the shop sends you to the address in the next parameter: https://shop.example/login?next=https://fake-shop.test. What is the risk?

opcoes.texto: None, the login is on the real shop
You end up on a fake site that looks like the shop
Login gets slower
Your cookies are deleted

cartoes.explicacao: The link starts on the real domain, which builds trust, and then takes the victim to the fake site. Accept only internal paths, like /account, or a fixed list of destinations.

cartoes.conceito: The Content-Security-Policy tells the browser which origins it may load scripts and other resources from.
cartoes.enunciado: Which HTTP header tells the browser where it may load scripts from, to stop XSS?
cartoes.explicacao: With script-src 'self', an injected inline script or one from another origin does not run. It is a second barrier: keep handling user text safely.

cartoes.conceito: A session cookie should have Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite.
cartoes.enunciado: Which of these headers creates a well-protected session cookie?

opcoes.texto: Set-Cookie: session=8f3a; Path=/
Set-Cookie: session=8f3a; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
Set-Cookie: session=8f3a; HttpOnly
Set-Cookie: session=8f3a; Secure; SameSite=None

cartoes.explicacao: Secure sends it only over HTTPS, HttpOnly hides it from JavaScript and SameSite=Lax does not send it with POSTs coming from other sites. Use all three on the session cookie.

cartoes.titulo: A session from start to finish
cartoes.conceito: The session id must be new after login and destroyed at logout.
cartoes.enunciado: Order the life cycle of a secure session, from first step to last.

itens.texto: The browser sends the cookie with every request
The server creates a new, random session id
At logout, the server deletes the session

cartoes.explicacao: Creating the id only after login stops an attacker from forcing an id they already know on you (session fixation). At logout, delete the session on the server, not just the cookie.

cartoes.conceito: Clickjacking: another site loads yours in an invisible iframe and tricks the user into clicking.
cartoes.enunciado: Which classic header stops other sites from loading yours inside an iframe?
cartoes.explicacao: With X-Frame-Options: DENY or the CSP directive frame-ancestors 'none', the browser refuses to show the site in someone else's iframe. Turn one of them on for every page.

cartoes.conceito: Reflecting any origin with credentials lets any site read responses on the user's behalf.
cartoes.enunciado: This API only serves the shop.example app. Which line exposes it to any site?
cartoes.explicacao: Accepting whatever origin arrives, with credentials, lets any site read the responses with the victim's cookies. Use a fixed list: origin: ['https://shop.example'].

cartoes.titulo: Two networks at the coffee shop
cartoes.conceito: Anyone can create a Wi-Fi network named after a coffee shop (evil twin).
cartoes.enunciado: At the coffee shop you see the networks 'Cafe_Central' and 'Cafe_Central_Free'. What do you do?

opcoes.texto: Pick the free one, it's open
Ask at the counter which one is official and only use HTTPS sites
Pick the one with the strongest signal
It doesn't matter, Wi-Fi is always encrypted

cartoes.explicacao: A fake network can see and change any traffic that is not encrypted. Check the name with the staff, prefer HTTPS or mobile data and avoid sensitive tasks.

cartoes.conceito: Every point between you and the site can see where you are going; HTTPS hides the content, not the destination.
cartoes.enunciado: Order the path of a request, from your laptop to the site.
cartoes.explicacao: The router and the internet provider see which sites you connect to and when, even with HTTPS. What HTTPS guarantees is that the content and the passwords stay encrypted all the way to the site.

cartoes.conceito: HSTS forces the browser to use HTTPS on a site, even if someone types http://.
cartoes.enunciado: Which mechanism tells the browser to always use HTTPS on a site, even if you type http:// in the address bar?
cartoes.explicacao: Without HSTS, the first request over http:// can be intercepted on a hostile network. Send Strict-Transport-Security with a long max-age on every HTTPS response.

cartoes.titulo: What happens when you open an HTTPS site
cartoes.conceito: Before any data is sent encrypted, the browser checks the server's certificate.
cartoes.enunciado: You open https://shop.example. Order the steps, from first to last.

itens.texto: A TCP connection to the server is opened
DNS translates shop.example into an IP address
The HTTP request is sent encrypted

cartoes.explicacao: If the certificate is not valid for shop.example, the browser stops before sending any data. Never ignore that warning.

cartoes.titulo: What a VPN does not do
cartoes.conceito: A VPN encrypts the path to the VPN server; it does not stop phishing or malware.
cartoes.enunciado: You turned on a VPN. What does it actually protect you from?

opcoes.texto: Phishing sites
People on the same Wi-Fi network seeing your traffic
Malware that is already on your laptop
The site knowing who you are after you log in

cartoes.explicacao: A VPN hides your traffic from the local network, but the VPN provider can now see it. For phishing and malware you need other defenses, such as MFA and updates.

cartoes.titulo: Too many ports open on the firewall
cartoes.conceito: A web server should only expose the ports it needs to the internet.
cartoes.enunciado: These are the firewall rules of a public web server. Which rules expose too much?
cartoes.explicacao: The database (3306) should never be open to the internet and SSH (22) should only accept the VPN or the team's IPs. Leave only ports 80 and 443 open.

cartoes.conceito: Traditional DNS travels unencrypted; DoH hides the names you look up.
cartoes.enunciado: Which acronym stands for DNS encrypted inside HTTPS?
cartoes.explicacao: Without encryption, anyone on the network can see and fake the names you ask for. Turn on encrypted DNS (DoH or DoT) in your browser or your system.

cartoes.titulo: Where to connect the cheap cameras
cartoes.conceito: Putting untrusted devices on their own network limits the damage if they are attacked.
cartoes.enunciado: You bought cheap Wi-Fi cameras for your home. Where do you connect them?

opcoes.texto: On the same network as your work laptop
On a separate network, like the guest network
Straight to the internet, without a router
On any network, as long as it has a password

cartoes.explicacao: If a camera is attacked, on a separate network it cannot reach your laptop or your files. Also change its factory password and update the firmware.

cartoes.conceito: WEP and WPS are well-known weak points in home Wi-Fi.
cartoes.enunciado: These are the router settings. Which lines weaken the network?
cartoes.explicacao: WEP can be cracked in minutes and the WPS PIN can be guessed by brute force. Use WPA3 (or WPA2) and turn WPS off.

cartoes.conceito: A certificate warning can be a sign that someone is intercepting the connection.
cartoes.enunciado: On the hotel Wi-Fi, the browser warns 'Your connection is not private' when you open shop.example. What do you do?

opcoes.texto: Click 'Proceed anyway'
Leave the page and do not type any data
Reload until the warning goes away
Turn off the antivirus

cartoes.explicacao: An invalid certificate can mean someone has put themselves in the middle of the connection. Leave, use mobile data and try again later.

cartoes.conceito: An app should only have the permissions it needs to work.
cartoes.enunciado: A calculator app asks for access. Which permission makes sense to give it?

opcoes.texto: Contacts
Precise location
Microphone
None of these

cartoes.explicacao: A calculator does not need to know who you know or where you are. Refuse what makes no sense and review permissions in your settings.

cartoes.titulo: The photo says where you are
cartoes.conceito: A photo's EXIF metadata can store the GPS coordinates of where it was taken.
cartoes.enunciado: What is the name of a photo's metadata that can store the date, the phone model and the GPS coordinates?
cartoes.explicacao: A photo shared as a file can reveal your address. Turn off location in the camera or remove the metadata before sending.

cartoes.conceito: A tracking pixel in an email tells the sender when and where you opened it.
cartoes.enunciado: A marketing email has an invisible 1×1 pixel image. What is it for?

opcoes.texto: Decoration
Finding out whether, when and where you opened the email
Making it load faster
Protecting against spam

cartoes.explicacao: When the image loads, your email program sends a request to the sender's server. Block remote images by default.

cartoes.conceito: The GDPR gives you the right to receive your data in a format another service can read.
cartoes.enunciado: Which GDPR right lets you take your data to another service, in a machine-readable format?
cartoes.explicacao: The right to data portability (Article 20) applies to the data you provided. Ask the service for it and import it into the new one.

cartoes.titulo: Too much data for a newsletter
cartoes.conceito: Data minimization: collect only the data you need for the stated purpose.
cartoes.enunciado: This form is only for signing up to the newsletter. Which fields ask for too much data?
segmentos: I agree to receive the newsletter
cartoes.explicacao: To send a newsletter, the email is enough. Data you do not collect cannot be stolen in a breach.

cartoes.titulo: Asking a company for your data
cartoes.conceito: The right of access lets you find out what data a company holds about you.
cartoes.enunciado: You want to know what data TelcoNet keeps about you. Order the steps.

itens.texto: You receive a copy of the data, usually within a month
You find the contact for the data protection officer
You ask for anything wrong to be corrected
You send the access request in writing

cartoes.explicacao: The data protection officer's contact is in the privacy policy. The company usually has one month to reply, and you can ask for anything wrong to be corrected.

cartoes.titulo: No cookies and they still recognize you
cartoes.conceito: Browser fingerprinting combines technical details that identify you without cookies.
cartoes.enunciado: You deleted all your cookies, but a site still recognizes you. How is that possible?

opcoes.texto: Browser fingerprinting: screen, fonts, version and other details
The site read your email
The Wi-Fi told the site
It was a coincidence

cartoes.explicacao: The combination of small browser details is almost unique. Use a browser with fingerprinting protection and few extensions.

cartoes.conceito: The barcode on a boarding pass contains your name and booking reference.
cartoes.enunciado: Which of these posts helps a scammer the most?

opcoes.texto: Photo of the sunset on the beach
Photo of your boarding pass with the barcode visible
Review of a movie
Photo of your cat

cartoes.explicacao: With your name and booking reference, someone can change or cancel your flight. Post after the trip and never show codes or documents.

cartoes.conceito: Personal data in a URL ends up in the history and in the logs of every server the request passes through.
cartoes.enunciado: This link was generated by a shop after you signed up. Which parts should not be in the URL?
cartoes.explicacao: The URL is saved in the history, in server and proxy logs and in analytics tools. Send personal data in the body of a POST request, over HTTPS.

cartoes.conceito: Each sharing level widens who sees what you post; the most restricted is the most private.
cartoes.enunciado: Order the sharing options, from most private to most public.
cartoes.explicacao: Friends of friends can be thousands of strangers. Choose Friends by default and review your old posts.

cartoes.conceito: CEO fraud: someone pretends to be a boss to ask for an urgent, secret transfer.
cartoes.enunciado: This email reached Atlas Corp's accounting team. What do you do?

cenario.label: Email received
lines: I need an urgent transfer of €18,000 to a new supplier.
I'm in a meeting, don't call me. Reply by email only.

opcoes.texto: Make the transfer, it's the CEO
Confirm by phone, using the internal number I already know
Reply to the email asking for more details
Ask a colleague to make the transfer

cartoes.explicacao: Urgency, secrecy and an address from outside the company are the classic signs. Always confirm through a channel you already know, never the one in the message.

cartoes.conceito: Tailgating: getting into a secure area by following closely behind someone who has access.
cartoes.enunciado: At the office door, someone carrying a heavy box asks you to hold the door. They have no badge in sight. What do you do?

opcoes.texto: Hold the door, it's polite
Offer to help and walk them to reception to sign in
Lend them my badge
Let them in and report it later

cartoes.explicacao: Being friendly does not mean opening the door. Send anyone without a badge to reception.

cartoes.conceito: Vishing: a voice-call scam where the scammer pretends to be from the bank or tech support.
cartoes.enunciado: Someone from 'Banco Luz support' calls and asks for the code you just received by SMS. How often does a real bank ask you for that code over the phone?
cartoes.explicacao: The code is for you to approve an operation; whoever asks for it wants to approve it for you. Hang up and call the number on the back of your card.

cartoes.conceito: MFA fatigue: the attacker already has the password and sends requests until someone approves one.
cartoes.enunciado: Your phone shows 15 requests in a row to approve a login you did not make. What do you do?

opcoes.texto: Approve one to make them stop
Deny them all, change my password and tell the security team
Turn off my phone and wait
Uninstall the authenticator app

cartoes.explicacao: The requests show that someone already knows your password. Deny them, change it right away and ask for MFA with number matching or a physical key.

cartoes.conceito: Pretexting: a believable story is used to ask for something you should never hand over.
cartoes.enunciado: You received these messages in the company chat. Which parts are warning signs?
segmentos: We're migrating the email accounts today.
I need your password to copy your mailbox.
The director wants this done by 5 pm.
cartoes.explicacao: IT never needs your password, and pressure from a boss is there to stop you thinking. Confirm the request through another channel and report it.

cartoes.titulo: The stages of a social engineering attack
cartoes.conceito: A social engineering attack starts long before contact: with research on the target.
cartoes.enunciado: Order the stages of the attack, from first to last.

itens.texto: Research the target on social media and the company website
Ask for the access, the data or the money
Build trust with a believable story

cartoes.explicacao: The more the attacker knows about you, the more believable the story. Share fewer work details in public.

cartoes.titulo: The USB drive in the parking lot
cartoes.conceito: Baiting: leaving a tempting object, like a USB drive, and waiting for someone to use it.
cartoes.enunciado: You find a USB drive in the company parking lot labeled 'Salaries 2026'. What do you do?

opcoes.texto: Plug it into my laptop to see whose it is
Hand it to the security team without plugging it in
Plug it into a computer at reception
Format it and keep it

cartoes.explicacao: A USB drive can run code as soon as it is plugged in, or pretend to be a keyboard. Hand it in without plugging it into anything.

cartoes.conceito: Spear phishing: phishing aimed at one person, with real details to look legitimate.
cartoes.enunciado: An email uses your name, your boss's name and the project you work on. What is this kind of targeted phishing called?
cartoes.explicacao: The details come from social media and data breaches, so looking personal proves nothing. Confirm unusual requests through another channel.

cartoes.conceito: Bank details fraud: an email asks you to pay into a new account and avoids any confirmation.
cartoes.enunciado: This email seems to come from a regular supplier. Which lines are signs of fraud?
segmentos: Good morning, here is the October invoice.
We've changed banks: please pay right away to the new IBAN attached.
Don't call, the phone line is under maintenance.
cartoes.explicacao: A change of bank account plus a request not to call is the pattern of this fraud. Always confirm by phone, using a number you already had.

cartoes.conceito: The 'I changed my number' scam uses family trust to ask for money in a hurry.
cartoes.enunciado: Order the stages of this messaging scam, from first to last.

itens.texto: Writes: 'Hi Mom, this is my new number'
Asks for money to pay an urgent bill
The victim sends the money without confirming by voice
Says the old phone broke and they can't call

cartoes.explicacao: The excuse for not being able to call is the key point. Call the old number or ask a question only the real person could answer.

cartoes.conceito: The Caesar cipher replaces each letter with another one a fixed distance away. With only 25 keys, it breaks in seconds.
cartoes.enunciado: You intercepted a message encrypted with the Caesar cipher, with a shift of 3. What does it say?
cartoes.verificacao: The validate must use the cesar function from ../../lib/hash.js: the right answer is cesar('DWWDFN DW QRRQ', -3). Compare with normalizar() on both sides, so that case and accents do not count.
cartoes.explicacao: Each letter moves back 3 places: D becomes A, W becomes T. An attacker tries all 25 keys in seconds. It is for learning, not for protecting.

cartoes.conceito: Base64 is a way of writing bytes as text, not a cipher: anyone can reverse it.
cartoes.enunciado: This cookie looks encrypted, but it is only Base64. What does it say once decoded?
cartoes.verificacao: The validate must use the deBase64 function from ../../lib/hash.js: the right answer is deBase64('cm9sZT1yZWFkZXI='). Compare with normalizar() on both sides.
cartoes.explicacao: Anyone can decode the cookie and swap it for role=admin. Keep the role on the server or sign the cookie, instead of trusting Base64.

cartoes.conceito: A SHA-256 hash changes completely if the file changes, so it is used to check downloads.
cartoes.enunciado: You downloaded the Atlas Corp installer from three places. Which file (A, B or C) has the SHA-256 published on the official site?
cartoes.verificacao: The validate must use the sha256Hex function from ../../lib/hash.js. Define FILES = { a: 'Atlas App 2.9.3 (modified)', b: 'Atlas App 2.9.3 (official)', c: 'Atlas App 2.9.2 (official)' } and PUBLISHED = '87131d4981f502852ee8408055118dda6716bd9566f320f67ca2483a787985ad'. The check strips an optional 'file ' from the start of the normalized answer and accepts it only if it is a key of FILES whose sha256Hex(content) equals PUBLISHED.
cartoes.explicacao: A single different byte changes the whole hash: compare the full hash, not just the start. And make sure the hash comes from the official site, over HTTPS.

cartoes.conceito: Without a salt, identical passwords give identical hashes and stand out in a breach.
cartoes.enunciado: In a breach, the passwords were stored with SHA-256 and no salt. Which two users have the same password?
cartoes.verificacao: The validate must use the sha256Hex function from ../../lib/hash.js. Define PASSWORDS = { ana: 'summer2026', tom: 'blue-cat-77', eva: 'summer2026' } and compute the sha256Hex of each one; the right names are the ones with a repeated hash. The check takes the words of the normalized answer that are keys of PASSWORDS and accepts it only if they are exactly those names, in any order.
cartoes.explicacao: Without a salt, the same password always gives the same hash. With a random salt per user and a slow algorithm like Argon2id, the hashes all come out different.

cartoes.conceito: Encryption can be reversed with the key; a hash is one-way.
cartoes.enunciado: What is the difference between encrypting and computing a hash?

opcoes.texto: They are the same thing with different names
Encryption can be reversed with the key; a hash cannot be reversed
A hash needs a secret key; encryption does not
A hash is always more secure than encryption

cartoes.explicacao: You encrypt what you will need to read again, like a file. For passwords you store a slow, salted hash, because you only need to compare.

cartoes.conceito: Avalanche effect: changing a single character in the input changes the whole hash.
cartoes.enunciado: These two texts differ only in one capital letter. How many of the first 10 characters of the two hashes are the same, in the same position?
cartoes.verificacao: The validate must use the sha256Hex function from ../../lib/hash.js. Compute sha256Hex('Atlas') and sha256Hex('atlas') and count the positions from 0 to 9 where the character is the same. Accept the normalized answer if it is that number, written in digits.
cartoes.explicacao: In a good hash, every character changes with the same probability, so any matches are pure chance. This is what stops anyone from guessing the input from similar-looking hashes.

cartoes.titulo: From the weakest key to the strongest
cartoes.conceito: Each extra bit in a key doubles the number of keys an attacker has to try.
cartoes.enunciado: Order these ciphers, from weakest key to strongest.
cartoes.explicacao: Caesar and DES break by brute force; AES-128 is already out of reach and AES-256 gives extra margin. Use AES with 128-bit or 256-bit keys.

cartoes.titulo: Storing passwords: from worst to best
cartoes.conceito: Passwords are stored with a slow, salted hash, designed on purpose to be costly to test.
cartoes.enunciado: Order these ways of storing passwords, from worst to best.
cartoes.explicacao: SHA-256 is too fast: a graphics card tries billions of guesses per second. Use Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt, which are slow on purpose.

cartoes.conceito: HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS; the old SSL is no longer secure.
cartoes.enunciado: Which protocol encrypts the connection when you see https:// in the browser's address bar?
cartoes.explicacao: SSL and the first versions of TLS have known flaws. Configure servers with TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only.

cartoes.conceito: Security tokens need a cryptographic random generator, not Math.random().
cartoes.enunciado: You are generating the token for a password reset link. Which do you use?

opcoes.texto: Math.random()
Date.now()
crypto.getRandomValues()
The user's email in Base64

cartoes.explicacao: Math.random() and the time are predictable, and the email in Base64 can be guessed. Use crypto.getRandomValues() or crypto.randomBytes() with at least 128 bits.

cartoes.conceito: Secrets written in the code end up in git and in every copy of the repository.
cartoes.enunciado: This configuration file is going into the repository. Which line exposes a secret?
cartoes.explicacao: Anyone with access to the repository, or to an old copy of it, gets the key. Read it from an environment variable or a secrets vault, as in process.env.API_KEY.

cartoes.titulo: I deleted the key in the next commit
cartoes.conceito: What goes into git stays in the history; an exposed key must be revoked.
cartoes.enunciado: You committed an API key and deleted it in the next commit. Is it fixed?

opcoes.texto: Yes, it's no longer in the code
No: it stays in the history; revoke the key and create a new one
Yes, if the repository is private
Just rename the variable

cartoes.explicacao: Every clone or fork keeps the old commit, and bots scan public repositories for keys. Revoke the key right away and only then clean the history.

cartoes.conceito: The .env file with secrets never goes into the repository; share only a .env.example without values.
cartoes.enunciado: Which git file says which files, like .env, must never go into the repository?
cartoes.explicacao: Put .env in .gitignore before the first commit and keep a .env.example with just the variable names. That way the team knows what to configure without seeing the values.

cartoes.titulo: From minimal access to full access
cartoes.conceito: Least privilege: each account or service gets only the access it needs.
cartoes.enunciado: Order these permissions on a bucket, from most restricted to broadest.

itens.texto: Read and write the whole bucket

cartoes.explicacao: If a service is compromised, the attacker gets only what that service could do. Start with minimal access and widen it only when needed.

cartoes.conceito: A bucket with public read access can be reached by anyone on the internet.
cartoes.enunciado: The atlas-backups bucket has public read access turned on. Who can read the backups?

opcoes.texto: Only the Atlas Corp team
Anyone on the internet who knows or guesses the name
Nobody, buckets are always private
Only people with an account at the same provider

cartoes.explicacao: Some people search for open buckets automatically, trying predictable names. Turn on public access blocking and grant access only to specific accounts.

cartoes.conceito: A secret has a life cycle: it is created in a vault, rotated regularly and revoked at the end.
cartoes.enunciado: Order the life cycle of an API key, from first step to last.

itens.texto: Give access only to the service that uses it
Revoke the key when the service is shut down
Create the key in the secrets vault

cartoes.explicacao: Rotating limits how long a stolen key is useful, and revoking it at the end avoids forgotten keys. Automate rotation in the secrets vault.

cartoes.titulo: The secret in the CI log
cartoes.conceito: Everything a pipeline prints ends up in the logs, which many people can read.
cartoes.enunciado: This CI pipeline runs on every push. Which step exposes a secret?
cartoes.explicacao: The echo writes the token to the logs, where it stays. Pass it as a CI secret to the tool that needs it and never print it.

cartoes.conceito: The main cloud account controls everything and needs the strongest protection.
cartoes.enunciado: Atlas Corp's cloud root account only has a password. What protection should you turn on right away?
cartoes.explicacao: Whoever gets into the root account can delete everything or create resources at your expense. Turn on MFA with a physical key and use accounts with fewer permissions day to day.

cartoes.conceito: A secret written in the Dockerfile is baked into the image, within reach of anyone who downloads it.
cartoes.enunciado: This image is going to a shared registry. Which line leaves a secret in it?
cartoes.explicacao: Anyone with the image can see the value with docker history or docker inspect. Pass the secret only when the container starts, from a secrets vault.

cartoes.titulo: How the app reaches the database
cartoes.conceito: Temporary credentials, given by the cloud to a service, avoid fixed keys that can leak.
cartoes.enunciado: A cloud app needs to read a database. Which credential is safest?

opcoes.texto: A fixed access key in the code
A role with temporary credentials managed by the cloud
The admin password, shared by the team
A key in a file on the desktop

cartoes.explicacao: Temporary credentials expire on their own and there is nothing fixed in the code to steal. Give the role only the read permissions the app needs.

cartoes.titulo: From the weakest lock to the strongest
cartoes.conceito: The more combinations a lock has, the longer it takes to guess.
cartoes.enunciado: Order these screen locks, from weakest to strongest.

itens.texto: Long password with letters and numbers

cartoes.explicacao: A 4-digit PIN has 10,000 combinations and a 6-digit one has a million. Use at least 6 digits or a password, with biometrics on top.

cartoes.conceito: Apps installed outside the official stores are the main way malware gets onto phones.
cartoes.enunciado: A friend sends you the APK of a paid game, 'for free'. What do you do?

opcoes.texto: Install it and turn on 'unknown sources'
Don't install it; use only the official store
Install it and then run an antivirus
Install it on an old phone

cartoes.explicacao: Pirated apps often carry hidden malware. Install only from the official store and keep installing from unknown sources turned off.

cartoes.conceito: The accessibility service lets an app read the screen and tap buttons for you.
cartoes.enunciado: An app to 'clean up your phone' asks for access to the accessibility service. Why is that dangerous?

opcoes.texto: It uses a lot of battery
It lets the app read the screen and tap buttons for you
It changes the font size
It is not dangerous

cartoes.explicacao: With this access, a malicious app reads codes and approves payments without you seeing. Give it only to accessibility apps you trust.

cartoes.conceito: Security updates fix flaws that attackers already know about.
cartoes.enunciado: Your phone has had a security update pending for three weeks. What do you do?

opcoes.texto: Wait for the next major version
Install it as soon as I can
Only update if I notice problems
Turn off updates

cartoes.explicacao: Once the fix is out, the flaw becomes public and attacks increase. Turn on automatic updates and replace your phone when it stops getting them.

cartoes.titulo: How a phone number gets stolen
cartoes.conceito: SIM swap: the attacker convinces the carrier to move your number to their own SIM card.
cartoes.enunciado: Order the stages of a SIM swap attack, from first to last.

itens.texto: The carrier activates the number on a new SIM
Calls the carrier pretending to be the victim
The attacker receives the victim's SMS codes

cartoes.explicacao: After the swap, every SMS code goes to the attacker. Ask your carrier, like TelcoNet, for a PIN for account changes and use an authenticator app instead of SMS.

cartoes.conceito: Locking and wiping remotely protects the data on a lost phone.
cartoes.enunciado: You lost your phone with your work email on it. What do you do first?

opcoes.texto: Wait for someone to return it
Lock it remotely, wipe it if needed and tell the company
Post on social media that I lost it
Buy another one and forget about it

cartoes.explicacao: With the find-my-device feature, you can locate, lock and wipe the phone. Tell the company so it can end any open sessions.

cartoes.titulo: Is the app ready for the store?
cartoes.conceito: A published app must not be in debug mode or accept unencrypted traffic.
cartoes.enunciado: This is the Android manifest for the version going to the store. Which lines are insecure?
cartoes.explicacao: Debug mode lets tools attach to the app, and unencrypted traffic can be read on the network. Publish with debuggable set to false and with HTTPS only.

cartoes.conceito: A public USB port can exchange data with your phone, not just power.
cartoes.enunciado: At the airport, you want to charge your phone. What is safest?

opcoes.texto: Use the USB port and accept 'Trust This Computer'
Use your own charger in a power outlet, or a USB data blocker
Use the USB port with Wi-Fi turned off
Use the USB port with the phone on silent

cartoes.explicacao: Only power goes through a power outlet. If you use a USB port, never accept 'Trust This Computer'.

cartoes.conceito: Mobile device management enforces security rules and lets the company wipe data remotely.
cartoes.enunciado: Which acronym names the system a company uses to require a screen lock on work phones and to wipe them remotely?
cartoes.explicacao: With MDM, the company requires a lock and encryption and can wipe only the work data if the phone is lost. On a personal phone, use a separate work profile.

cartoes.titulo: What shows on the lock screen
cartoes.conceito: Notifications on the lock screen can show codes to anyone who picks up the phone.
cartoes.enunciado: This is your phone's lock screen. Which notification should not appear like this?
segmentos: Banco Luz: your confirmation code is 482913
cartoes.explicacao: Anyone who picks up the phone can read the code without unlocking it. Set notifications to hide their content on the lock screen.

cartoes.conceito: Joining a file name that comes from the user onto a path lets it escape the intended folder.
cartoes.enunciado: This endpoint serves files from the uploads folder. Which line lets someone read files outside that folder?
cartoes.explicacao: With file=../../etc/passwd, the path escapes the uploads folder. Use path.basename(name) or check that the resolved path starts with /srv/uploads/.

cartoes.conceito: Validating against a list of what is allowed is safer than trying to block what is dangerous.
cartoes.enunciado: A form asks for your age. What is the best validation on the server?

opcoes.texto: Remove the < and > characters
Accept only whole numbers between 0 and 130
Validate only in the browser, with JavaScript
Accept anything and deal with it later

cartoes.explicacao: Defining what is valid shuts the door on everything else, including tricks you did not foresee. Browser validation helps the user, but the server has to repeat all of it.

cartoes.conceito: Passwords and tokens must never go into the application logs.
cartoes.enunciado: This code logs every login. Which line puts secret data in the logs?
cartoes.explicacao: Logs are read by many people and tools and kept for months. Log the event and the user, never the password or the token.

cartoes.conceito: eval() runs any text it receives as code.
cartoes.enunciado: A web calculator runs eval(input) on whatever the user types. Why is that dangerous?

opcoes.texto: It is slow
It runs any code the user types
It does not accept decimal numbers
It does not work on phones

cartoes.explicacao: Anyone who types code instead of a sum can run it. Use an expression parser that accepts only numbers and operators.

cartoes.conceito: A dependency with a known flaw is fixed by updating it, with tests before the deploy.
cartoes.enunciado: npm audit warns that a dependency has a known flaw. Order the steps to fix it.

itens.texto: Update the version in package.json and in the lockfile
Read the advisory and find which version fixes the flaw

cartoes.explicacao: A published flaw gets exploited fast, so updating is urgent, but the tests keep you from breaking the app. Automate the alerts with npm audit or a dependency bot.

cartoes.titulo: Values kept apart from the SQL
cartoes.conceito: Parameterized queries send the SQL and the values separately, and the database never mixes them.
cartoes.enunciado: What is the technique called where you write the SQL with placeholders (like ?) and send the values separately?
cartoes.explicacao: The value is never read as SQL, so ' OR '1'='1 stays plain text. Use them in every query, even the ones that look safe.

cartoes.titulo: The error that says too much
cartoes.conceito: Detailed error messages show the attacker how the application works inside.
cartoes.enunciado: This is the API's error handler. Which line reveals internal details to whoever made the request?
cartoes.explicacao: The stack trace shows paths, versions and parts of the code. Log the details on the server and return only a generic message with an error id.

cartoes.conceito: Without a limit on attempts, the login is open to brute-force attacks.
cartoes.enunciado: The /login endpoint accepts unlimited requests. Which attack becomes easier?

opcoes.texto: Password brute force
XSS
Path traversal
None, the login is protected by the password

cartoes.explicacao: A bot can try thousands of passwords per minute. Limit attempts per account and per IP and add increasing delays.

cartoes.conceito: Gluing user text onto a shell command lets other commands run.
cartoes.enunciado: This endpoint pings a server. Which line allows command injection?
cartoes.explicacao: With host=example.com; ls, the shell runs a second command. Use execFile('ping', ['-c', '1', host]), which does not go through the shell, and validate the host.

cartoes.conceito: The lockfile pins the exact versions of every dependency, including indirect ones.
cartoes.enunciado: In npm, which file pins the exact versions of all installed dependencies?
cartoes.explicacao: With the lockfile in git, everyone installs exactly the same code, the code that was audited. Use npm ci in CI and review lockfile changes.
